746373.hinge: Isolated peripheral blueness of hands, feet, and perioral skin with normal vitality and pink mucous membranes in the first 24-48 hours is benign physiologic acrocyanosis.
746373.trap: Perioral cyanosis can mimic central cyanosis from congenital heart disease, but oral mucosal pinkness and normal Apgar scores confirm acrocyanosis.

A.fit: Here: 4 hours old, cyanosis of hands and feet, normal exam

nodes.text: Blue hands, feet, perioral skin; pink tongue; vigorous newborn: acrocyanosis
Transient peripheral vasomotor instability in first 24–48 hours
Warmth, skin-to-skin contact, reassurance
**Blue tongue or mucosa (central cyanosis):** pre/postductal oximetry, hyperoxia test, echocardiogram
**PaO2 does not rise with 100% oxygen:** cyanotic heart disease — prostaglandin E1 if ductal-dependent
**Chocolate-brown blood with normal PaO2:** methemoglobinemia — co-oximetry
Routine CCHD pulse oximetry screen at ≥ 24 hours

746374.trap: Tachypnea suggests respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis, but PCO2 is elevated (50 mm Hg), proving respiratory failure.

A.fit: Not here: PCO2 is elevated at 50 mm Hg, not decreased

nodes.text: Parents of child with life-threatening illness request substituting unproven alternative therapies for standard curative treatment
Acknowledge parental fears regarding chemotherapy adverse effects and explore cultural beliefs with empathy
Advise them to continue her medications while investigating the information further regarding drug interactions and toxicity
Explain the proven efficacy and survival benefits of standard leukemia chemotherapy protocols
**Parents persistently refuse life-saving therapy despite counseling:** obtain hospital ethics consultation and seek court-ordered treatment
Arrange close follow-up and offer supportive care to alleviate chemotherapy-induced nausea and adverse symptoms

abnormal-uterine-bleeding.name: Abnormal uterine bleeding
abnormal-uterine-bleeding.scope: Adenomyosis, leiomyomas, endometrial polyps, ovulatory dysfunction, PALM-COEIN classification, endometrial biopsy
abnormal-uterine-bleeding.core: Abnormal uterine bleeding requires pregnancy exclusion, hemodynamic assessment and evaluation for structural disease or unopposed endometrial estrogen.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Perimenopause, PCOS, obesity, anticoagulants; lifelong heavy bleeding suggests inherited coagulopathy
Adenomyosis often multiparous; fibroids common during reproductive years

rows.label: Clues
items: Bleeding affecting quality of life, prolonged/heavy menses, intermenstrual or irregular bleeding
Tachycardia, orthostasis or syncope → clinically important blood loss
Postmenopausal bleeding requires malignancy evaluation even with a single episode

rows.label: Pathophys
items: PALM: Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy/hyperplasia → structural causes
COEIN: Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not otherwise classified
Anovulation → absent cyclic progesterone, unopposed proliferation and unstable shedding
Combined OCPs → uniform estrogen/progestin exposure **synchronizes endometrium**, preventing irregular shedding

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pregnancy test and CBC** first; pelvic examination localizes uterine versus cervical/vaginal bleeding
**Transvaginal ultrasound** evaluates structural lesions; saline sonohysterography/hysteroscopy for intracavitary disease
★ **Endometrial biopsy ≥45 years**; younger with persistent bleeding, unopposed estrogen or failed treatment
Postmenopausal bleeding: endometrial thickness >4 mm → sampling; persistent bleeding → biopsy regardless of thickness
TSH for suspected endocrine disease; coagulation/vWF testing for suggestive bleeding history

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Unstable → IV access, blood resuscitation, urgent gynecology; tamponade or operative control if needed
Stable → high-dose combined OCP, progestin, tranexamic acid; no estrogen if prior VTE, hypertension, smoker >35
★ Long-term → **levonorgestrel IUD**, OCP/progestin; family complete, normal cavity → **ablation**; copper worsens
Fibroids: asymptomatic → **observation, any size**; symptomatic → myomectomy/embolization; hysterectomy if childbearing done
Polyp → hysteroscopic removal; adenomyosis refractory to hormones → hysterectomy

rows.label: Complications
items: Iron deficiency anemia; chronic anovulation → endometrial hyperplasia/cancer; structural lesions can impair fertility

rows.label: Prevention
items: Regular progestin exposure for chronic anovulation; replace iron and address metabolic drivers

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pregnancy complication: positive hCG; exclude ectopic pregnancy
Cervicitis: friable cervix and postcoital bleeding

table.title: Cause clues
rows: Firm irregular enlarged uterus; pressure symptoms
Labor-like pain, dilated os, beefy prolapsing tissue
Tender uterus; biopsy **plasma cells**, not neutrophils

acid-base-disorders.name: Acid-base disorders
acid-base-disorders.scope: Metabolic acidosis (anion gap, non-anion gap), metabolic alkalosis (saline-responsive vs saline-resistant), respiratory acidosis, respiratory alkalosis, Winter formula, mixed disorders
acid-base-disorders.core: Identify the primary pH disturbance, test expected compensation, then investigate the anion gap or urine chloride to locate the cause.

rows.label: Definition
items: Acidemia: pH <7.35; alkalemia: >7.45; normal pH can hide opposing primary disorders
Metabolic: primary HCO3 change; respiratory: primary PaCO2 change

rows.label: Formula
items: ★ **AG = Na − (Cl + HCO3)**; usual normal ≈8–12, laboratory dependent
Hypoalbuminemia correction: add 2.5 to AG per 1 g/dL albumin below 4
★ **Winter: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3 + 8 ±2**

rows.label: Interpret
items: HCO3 12 → expected PaCO2 26 ±2; measured 40 → additional respiratory acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis: expected PaCO2 ≈40 + 0.7 × (HCO3 − 24), ±5
Respiratory HCO3 change per 10 PaCO2: acidosis +1 acute/+4 chronic; alkalosis −2 acute/−4 chronic

rows.label: Use when
items: ★ Alkalosis: **urine Cl <20 mmol/L** → saline-responsive; ≥20 → diuretics/mineralocorticoids
ΔAG exceeds HCO3 fall → additional alkalosis; smaller ΔAG → additional non-gap acidosis

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Compensation never overshoots; values outside expected range imply **mixed disorder**
Salicylates often cause respiratory alkalosis plus high-gap acidosis; near-normal pH is deceptive
Diarrhea/RTA: non-gap acidosis; distal RTA: urine pH >5.5, hypokalemia; renal failure: either gap pattern

acid-base-disorders.evidence: Established physiologic formulas; no guideline involved.

airway-management.name: Airway management
airway-management.scope: Indications for endotracheal intubation (GCS <= 8, airway protection, respiratory failure), rapid sequence intubation, bag-valve-mask ventilation, difficult airway
airway-management.core: Secure the airway when oxygenation, ventilation, or protection fails; preparation and rescue oxygenation determine safety.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Facial/neck trauma, burns, angioedema, obesity, limited jaw opening or cervical mobility
Shock, severe hypoxemia, metabolic acidosis increase peri-intubation collapse risk

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **GCS ≤8**, absent protective reflexes, recurrent aspiration, apnea → assess need for definitive airway
Stridor, fatigue, rising CO₂, refractory hypoxemia, inability to handle secretions → impending failure
GCS alone imperfect: reversible intoxication without ventilation/protection failure may permit closely monitored observation
Toxic sore throat, drooling, stridor → epiglottitis: laryngoscopy + intubation in OR before imaging/cultures

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Upper-airway obstruction, depressed drive, or respiratory muscle failure prevents effective gas exchange
Induction/positive pressure reduces sympathetic tone and venous return, worsening hypotension

rows.label: Dx
items: Continuous pulse oximetry, ECG, BP; assess mouth opening, neck anatomy, aspiration risk
★ Confirm tracheal placement with **persistent waveform capnography**, then auscultation and chest radiograph for depth
Do not rely on chest movement, oxygen saturation, or auscultation alone

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Position, suction, **preoxygenate**; prepare BVM, supraglottic device, video laryngoscope, and surgical rescue
Two-person BVM with airway adjunct and oxygen; oral adjunct only without gag reflex
RSI: etomidate/ketamine + rocuronium/succinylcholine; provide immediate postintubation analgesia and sedation
★ Predicted difficult airway → awake intubation strategy; **cannot intubate/cannot oxygenate or shattered midface/mandible → cricothyrotomy**
Avoid succinylcholine: hyperkalemia, denervation, established major burns, neuromuscular disease, malignant hyperthermia risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Esophageal intubation, aspiration, dental injury, hypoxemia, cardiac arrest
Positive-pressure ventilation → barotrauma; prolonged ventilation → pneumonia, laryngeal injury
Right-mainstem tube → occludes right upper lobe bronchus → **alveolar collapse** (atelectasis), not air trapping
Prolonged intubation → **tracheomalacia**: dynamic expiratory collapse, localized wheeze, exertional dyspnea; not asthma

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Optimize **hemodynamics before induction**, use attempt limits and explicit backup plan
Head-of-bed elevation, oral care, daily sedation/ventilator liberation assessment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic hyperventilation: preserved oxygenation/protection, respiratory alkalosis
Compensatory Kussmaul breathing: metabolic acidosis; losing minute ventilation can cause abrupt deterioration

airway-management.evidence: Not checked online; established emergency airway principles.

asplenia.name: Asplenia
asplenia.scope: Anatomic asplenia (splenectomy), functional asplenia (sickle cell), Howell-Jolly bodies, reactive thrombocytosis, encapsulated organism sepsis (Streptococcus pneumoniae), vaccination timing, antibiotic prophylaxis
asplenia.core: Absent or poorly functioning spleen impairs clearance of encapsulated organisms; fever can progress rapidly to fatal sepsis despite prior vaccination.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Splenectomy for trauma/hematologic disease; functional loss with sickle cell disease; congenital absence
Sepsis risk greatest early after surgery and in children, but remains lifelong

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Fever, rigors, malaise, vomiting, or rapid deterioration → **overwhelming postsplenectomy infection**
Pneumococcus especially important; also meningococcus, Hib; dog bites risk Capnocytophaga
Travel-associated malaria and Babesia can become unusually severe

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Loss of splenic macrophage filtration and IgM memory B-cell function impairs opsonized-organism clearance
Reduced removal of erythrocyte inclusions and platelets explains characteristic blood findings

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Smear: **Howell–Jolly bodies**; reactive thrombocytosis after splenectomy; correlate with history/imaging
Febrile illness → cultures, CBC, lactate, source evaluation; do not delay antibiotics for results
Unexplained anemia/fever after tick exposure or travel → smear/PCR for intraerythrocytic parasites

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected sepsis → **immediate ceftriaxone**, add vancomycin for severe/resistant pneumococcal concern
Resuscitate and admit if ill; even initially mild fever requires urgent clinical evaluation
Standby oral antibiotic if immediate care inaccessible, followed by emergency evaluation; not a substitute for assessment
Daily penicillin/amoxicillin in young children, particularly sickle cell disease through at least age 5

rows.label: Complications
items: Fulminant bacteremia, meningitis, purpura fulminans, DIC, death
Postoperative thrombosis risk; isolated reactive platelet elevation does not automatically require antiplatelet treatment

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Vaccinate **≥14 days before elective splenectomy**; after emergency surgery vaccinate once stable
Adult antibiotic prophylaxis individualized by postoperative period, immune status, and prior invasive infection
Medical alert ID, fever plan, influenza vaccination; bite counseling, travel precautions and malaria prevention

rows.label: Mimics
items: Iron deficiency: reactive thrombocytosis without splenic dysfunction
Hyposplenism: spleen present but impaired; similar infection precautions

table.title: Vaccine priorities: unvaccinated adults
rows: One dose if not previously vaccinated

atopic-dermatitis.name: Atopic dermatitis
atopic-dermatitis.scope: Atopic dermatitis, pruritus, flexural lichenification, emollients and topical corticosteroids, complications (eczema herpeticum, bacterial infection)
atopic-dermatitis.core: Chronic relapsing itchy eczema with xerosis; infants often have facial/extensor disease, while older children develop flexural lichenification.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Personal/family atopy, impaired skin barrier, dry climate; soaps, wool, fragrances, heat can trigger flares
Asthma and allergic rhinitis commonly coexist; scratching and bacterial colonization exacerbate inflammation

rows.label: Clues
items: Excoriations, erythema, oozing during flares; sleep disturbance and chronic thickening from rubbing
★ **Painful monomorphic punched-out erosions**, fever, rapid spread → eczema herpeticum
Honey-colored crusts, pustules, warmth or spreading erythema → secondary bacterial infection

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Barrier dysfunction increases water loss and allergen penetration; type 2 inflammation drives itch–scratch cycle

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis** by itch, distribution, chronicity; no routine serum IgE/food allergy panels
Atypical/refractory disease → assess contact allergy, infestation, immune deficiency; selected patch testing
Suspected HSV complication → lesion PCR, but begin treatment before results if clinically convincing

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Daily **thick emollient**, short lukewarm bathing, fragrance-free cleanser; apply moisturizer promptly afterward
★ Flares → **topical corticosteroid**, potency by site/severity: triamcinolone on body; hydrocortisone on face/folds
Tacrolimus/pimecrolimus for sensitive sites or steroid-sparing maintenance; wet wraps for selected severe flares
Refractory moderate/severe disease → phototherapy or dupilumab; avoid chronic systemic glucocorticoids
★ Eczema herpeticum → **systemic acyclovir** now; ocular involvement → ophthalmology

rows.label: Complications
items: S aureus superinfection, disseminated HSV, sleep loss, psychosocial burden
Excess topical steroid potency/duration → skin atrophy, striae; dupilumab → conjunctivitis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Barrier care, trigger reduction, short nails; intermittent maintenance anti-inflammatory treatment at recurrent sites
No empiric elimination diets without confirmed clinical allergy; avoid routine antibiotics for uninfected eczema

rows.label: Mimics
items: Contact dermatitis: exposure-shaped distribution, patch-test association
Scabies: nocturnal household itch, burrows in webs/wrists
Seborrheic dermatitis: greasy scale, less itching

carbon-monoxide-poisoning.name: Carbon monoxide poisoning
carbon-monoxide-poisoning.scope: Carboxyhemoglobin, pulse oximetry pitfall, normobaric and hyperbaric oxygen indications, delayed neurologic sequelae
carbon-monoxide-poisoning.core: Headache, dizziness, nausea, or confusion affecting several people in an enclosed combustion setting suggests carbon monoxide exposure.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: House fires, faulty heaters, generators indoors, vehicle exhaust, poorly ventilated fuel-burning equipment
Pregnancy, infancy, anemia, and cardiopulmonary disease increase vulnerability at a given exposure

rows.label: Clues
items: Odorless gas: flulike illness without fever; symptoms improve outside exposure site
★ **Syncope, altered consciousness, focal deficits, chest pain**, or severe acidosis → serious toxicity
**Cherry-red/flushed skin, pink mucosa** + indoor coma → suspect CO; often absent, normal color not reassuring

rows.label: Pathophys
items: CO binds hemoglobin avidly, reduces oxygen carriage, shifts dissociation curve left
Mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammation add tissue injury; fetal hemoglobin retains CO longer

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Venous or arterial co-oximetry** measures carboxyhemoglobin; draw promptly without delaying oxygen
★ **Normal pulse oximetry and PaO₂ do not exclude poisoning**; both can appear reassuring
COHb >2% in nonsmokers or >9% in smokers supports exposure; level poorly predicts outcome
ECG, troponin for cardiac injury; lactate/ABG for acidosis; pregnancy testing when relevant
Prior oxygen or delayed presentation lowers COHb; exposure history remains decisive

rows.label: Tx
items: Remove from source, protect rescuers, assess airway and ventilation
★ **100% oxygen by nonrebreather** immediately; intubate for coma or respiratory failure
Consider hyperbaric oxygen for neurologic impairment, loss of consciousness, cardiac injury, severe acidosis, or COHb >25–30%
Pregnancy → urgent hyperbaric consultation at lower severity/levels; treatment decisions integrate symptoms, not COHb alone
Smoke inhalation + profound lactic acidosis/shock → consider cyanide, give hydroxocobalamin

rows.label: Complications
items: Myocardial ischemia, arrhythmias, death; delayed cognitive, behavioral, gait, or movement deficits after recovery
Follow-up for delayed neurologic symptoms; mild initial presentation does not exclude later deficits

rows.label: Prevention
items: Working CO detectors, professional heater inspection, never run generators or engines indoors
Public safety evaluation before returning to the exposure site

rows.label: Mimics
items: Viral illness: fever and infectious contacts rather than shared building exposure
Methemoglobinemia: cyanosis, saturation near 85%, chocolate-colored blood
Cyanide poisoning: rapid collapse, marked lactate elevation after enclosed fire

childhood-and-adolescent-immunizations.name: Childhood and adolescent immunizations
childhood-and-adolescent-immunizations.scope: Routine pediatric vaccine schedule, adolescent immunizations (meningococcal conjugate, HPV, Tdap), catch-up vaccination guidelines
childhood-and-adolescent-immunizations.core: Vaccinate before exposure; use age, prior doses, minimum intervals, and immune status to choose the next dose.

rows.label: Who
items: All children; AAP 2026 schedule retains broad routine childhood protection

rows.label: Schedule
items: ★ 11–12 years: **Tdap, MenACWY**; MenACWY booster at 16 years
AAP HPV: start 9–12 years; <15 years → two doses, 6–12 months apart
HPV initiation ≥15 years or immunocompromised → three doses at 0, 1–2, 6 months

rows.label: Special groups
items: ★ Catch-up: **never restart**; respect minimum ages and intervals
Asplenia/complement defects: extra meningococcal/pneumococcal doses; annual influenza from 6 months
HBsAg-positive mother: HepB vaccine + HBIG within 12 hours of birth

rows.label: Choice
items: MenB: shared decision, usually 16–23 years; high-risk patients need earlier protection

rows.label: Contraindications
items: ★ Live vaccines: pregnancy, severe immunodeficiency; **conjugates (Hib) still indicated**; prior anaphylaxis: no repeat
Rotavirus: SCID, prior intussusception; first dose ≤14 weeks 6 days; finish by 8 months

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **AAP/classic boards: multidose HPV**; federal 2026 policy: one dose
Preterm → **chronological age, full dose**; mild illness, antibiotics, breastfeeding → vaccinate
Separate injectable live vaccines ≥4 weeks unless simultaneous; IVIG can delay MMR/varicella

table.title: Routine AAP childhood schedule
rows: First vaccination <9 years: two ≥4 weeks apart

complement-deficiencies.name: Complement deficiencies
complement-deficiencies.scope: Terminal (C5-C9) deficiency, early complement deficiency and SLE, C1 inhibitor deficiency
complement-deficiencies.core: Recurrent encapsulated infections, lupus-like autoimmunity, or nonurticarial angioedema can identify distinct defects in complement function.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Inherited complement mutations; family history of invasive bacterial infection or episodic swelling
Acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency: lymphoproliferative/autoimmune disease; eculizumab produces functional terminal blockade

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Recurrent Neisseria** infection → suspect terminal **C5–C9 deficiency**
Early classical-pathway deficiency: photosensitive rash, arthritis, nephritis with bacterial infections
★ Angioedema **without hives or itching**: facial/laryngeal swelling, severe episodic abdominal pain

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Complement supports opsonization, immune-complex clearance, and bacterial membrane injury
C1 inhibitor loss → uncontrolled kallikrein and excess bradykinin, rather than histamine release

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CH50 and AH50** screen classical and alternative pathway function; follow with individual component levels
Suspected hereditary angioedema → low C4, C1 inhibitor antigen and function
Acquired form often has low C1q; hereditary form generally preserves C1q

rows.label: Tx
items: Invasive infection → immediate IV ceftriaxone, cultures, sepsis support
★ Bradykinin attack: **C1 inhibitor concentrate or icatibant**; secure threatened airway early
Antihistamines, epinephrine, and corticosteroids do not reliably reverse hereditary attacks
Frequent angioedema → lanadelumab or prophylactic C1 inhibitor; specialist-guided plans before procedures

rows.label: Complications
items: Meningococcal sepsis/meningitis, recurrent pneumococcal infection; autoimmune renal injury
Laryngeal obstruction; bowel-wall edema can mimic a surgical abdomen

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **MenACWY + MenB**, pneumococcal and Hib vaccination; consider antibiotic prophylaxis for recurrent infections
Family screening; avoid ACE inhibitors and estrogen with hereditary angioedema

rows.label: Mimics
items: Histaminergic angioedema: urticaria, pruritus, allergen exposure, epinephrine response
Antibody deficiency: recurrent sinopulmonary disease with reduced immunoglobulins

complement-deficiencies.evidence: Not checked online; established immunology teaching.

congenital-abdominal-wall-defects.name: Congenital abdominal wall defects
congenital-abdominal-wall-defects.scope: Gastroschisis, omphalocele, elevated maternal serum AFP, umbilical cord insertion, peritoneal membrane coverage, associated anomalies, delivery and surgical reduction
congenital-abdominal-wall-defects.core: Prenatal ultrasound identifies herniated abdominal contents; defect location, covering membrane, and cord insertion distinguish gastroschisis from omphalocele.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Gastroschisis: young maternal age, smoking; usually sporadic
Omphalocele: associated aneuploidy and syndromic disease rather than an isolated bowel defect

rows.label: Clues
items: Prenatal external bowel loops; elevated maternal serum AFP, often higher with uncovered defects
★ **Omphalocele plus macroglossia/overgrowth** → consider Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and neonatal hypoglycemia
Exposed bowel after birth → rapid heat and fluid loss; inspect bowel perfusion

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Gastroschisis: paraumbilical wall defect allows direct amniotic exposure and bowel inflammation
Omphalocele: failure of herniated viscera to return to abdominal cavity during development

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Detailed fetal ultrasound** identifies anatomy and associated defects; fetal echocardiogram especially for omphalocele
Omphalocele → **fetal karyotype/microarray** by amniocentesis, genetic counseling; monitor fetal growth, fluid, and bowel appearance
Early normal physiologic midgut herniation should resolve by approximately 12 weeks; avoid premature labeling

rows.label: Tx
items: Plan delivery at center with neonatal surgery; cesarean not routine for uncomplicated gastroschisis
Large liver-containing omphalocele may favor cesarean to protect sac; individualize timing and route
★ Birth: **sterile warm saline covering/plastic bowel bag**, radiant warmer, IV fluids, antibiotics
★ **NPO + orogastric decompression**; protect mesentery from torsion, assess respiratory compromise
Primary surgical reduction/closure if tolerated; staged silo reduction when abdominal capacity limited

rows.label: Complications
items: Bowel ischemia/atresia, sepsis, prolonged ileus, short-bowel syndrome, parenteral nutrition-associated cholestasis
Forceful reduction → abdominal compartment syndrome, impaired ventilation and venous return

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation, prenatal care; no proven specific intervention prevents most cases

rows.label: Mimics
items: Umbilical hernia: skin-covered postnatal bulge, usually closes spontaneously
Bladder exstrophy: infraumbilical exposed bladder mucosa rather than herniated bowel

congenital-abdominal-wall-defects.evidence: Not checked online; established fetal-anatomy and neonatal surgical stabilization teaching.

congenital-heart-disease.name: Congenital heart disease
congenital-heart-disease.scope: Cyanotic heart disease (5 Ts: Tetralogy of Fallot, TGA, truncus, tricuspid atresia, TAPVR), acyanotic heart disease (VSD, ASD, PDA, coarctation of aorta), hyperoxia test, prostaglandin E1
congenital-heart-disease.core: Neonatal cyanosis or shock as the ductus closes demands urgent assessment for duct-dependent congenital heart disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Maternal diabetes, congenital rubella, family history; Down syndrome → AV septal defects
Prematurity → PDA; Turner syndrome → coarctation

rows.label: Clues
items: Poor feeding, diaphoresis, tachypnea, hepatomegaly → infant heart failure
VSD: harsh holosystolic lower-left sternal murmur; ASD: **fixed split S2**, pulmonic flow murmur, RV volume overload
PDA: continuous machinery murmur, bounding pulses; coarctation: weak femoral pulses, arm–leg BP gradient
Central cyanosis: blue lips/tongue, warm extremities → **low arterial saturation**; peripheral: cold extremities

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Left-to-right shunts (VSD, ASD, extracardiac PDA) increase pulmonary flow; remodeling can reverse flow → Eisenmenger syndrome
Duct-dependent lesions require pulmonary/systemic flow or mixing through fetal communications
High neonatal PVR limits VSD shunt → murmur appears/louder over weeks as **PVR falls**

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Preductal/right-hand and postductal/foot oxygen saturation; **echocardiography** defines anatomy
★ Hyperoxia test: little PaO2 rise with 100% oxygen suggests cardiac shunting; echo preferred
ECG and chest radiograph support diagnosis; normal murmur does not exclude critical disease

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected duct-dependent lesion → **prostaglandin E1** immediately; monitor for apnea
★ Tet spell (agitation, softer murmur) → knee–chest, oxygen, fluids, morphine; refractory → phenylephrine or propranolol
TGA with inadequate mixing → balloon atrial septostomy, then arterial switch
Large shunts → diuretics, closure; premature PDA → ibuprofen; **obstructed TAPVR → emergency repair**
Coarctation → repair; post-repair paradoxical hypertension → **IV beta-blocker**; Eisenmenger → **do not close shunt**

rows.label: Complications
items: Pulmonary hypertension, failure to thrive, arrhythmias, infective endocarditis
Right-to-left shunting → brain abscess, paradoxical emboli, secondary erythrocytosis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Pulse-ox newborn screening; rubella immunization before pregnancy; maternal glycemic control
Endocarditis prophylaxis for selected unrepaired cyanotic or prosthetic-material lesions during dental procedures

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lung disease: substantial oxygen response, pulmonary findings
PPHN: elevated pulmonary resistance with structurally normal heart

table.title: Five cyanotic lesions
rows: RV obstruction, VSD, overriding aorta, RVH; boot-shaped heart
Parallel circuits; single S2; egg-on-string silhouette
Pulmonary veins drain systemically; obstruction → edema

congenital-heart-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric cardiology teaching.

corneal-abrasion.name: Corneal abrasion
corneal-abrasion.scope: Corneal abrasion, corneal foreign body, fluorescein examination, topical antibiotics, tetanus prophylaxis, chemical eye injury
corneal-abrasion.core: Acute painful red eye after surface trauma; exclude an open globe, retained foreign body, and infectious keratitis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Fingernail or plant injury, airborne debris, contact lenses, eye rubbing
High-velocity metalwork suggests intraocular foreign body; alkali exposure penetrates deeply

rows.label: Clues
items: Foreign-body sensation, tearing, photophobia, blepharospasm; vision usually preserved unless central involvement
★ Reduced visual acuity, irregular pupil, hyphema, severe mechanism → urgent ophthalmology
Vertical linear scratches suggest retained material beneath upper eyelid

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Epithelial loss exposes densely innervated cornea; superficial defects generally heal within 24–48 hours
Chemical injury damages epithelium; severe alkali exposure causes stromal and limbal ischemia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Visual acuity → slit-lamp/**fluorescein** examination; evert upper lid for retained particles
Positive Seidel sign: aqueous streaming through fluorescein → open globe; avoid tonometry or manipulation
Suspected intraocular foreign body → orbital CT; avoid MRI if metal possible
Persistent pain beyond expected healing → reassess for ulcer, foreign body, or recurrent erosion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Chemical exposure → immediate copious irrigation; remove particles, continue until stable physiologic pH
Loose surface foreign body → saline irrigation/moistened swab; embedded object or rust ring → trained removal
★ Uncomplicated abrasion → topical **erythromycin**; contact lens-related → ciprofloxacin/ofloxacin for Pseudomonas
Oral NSAID/acetaminophen; no pressure patching or routine take-home topical anesthetic; avoid topical steroids
Open globe → rigid shield, NPO, IV antibiotics, emergency ophthalmology; never remove protruding object

rows.label: Complications
items: Bacterial keratitis, corneal ulcer, scarring, recurrent corneal erosion
Chemical burns: limbal stem-cell loss, corneal melting, glaucoma, permanent visual impairment

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Eye protection; stop contacts until healed; replace contaminated lenses and case
Tetanus prophylaxis: penetrating/contaminated wounds by vaccine history; unnecessary for clean superficial abrasion
Contact lens injury, large/central defect, persistent symptoms → review within 24 hours

rows.label: Mimics
items: HSV keratitis: dendritic fluorescein pattern with terminal bulbs
Corneal ulcer: white stromal infiltrate with epithelial defect
Acute angle closure: fixed mid-dilated pupil, markedly elevated IOP

dermatophyte-infections.name: Dermatophyte infections
dermatophyte-infections.scope: Tinea capitis, tinea corporis, tinea pedis, tinea cruris, onychomycosis, potassium hydroxide preparation, oral and topical antifungals
dermatophyte-infections.core: Keratin-invading fungi cause scaly skin lesions or infected hair/nails; the anatomic site determines topical versus systemic treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Warm humid conditions, occlusive footwear, shared showers, wrestling, infected animals or contacts
Diabetes, immunosuppression; childhood favors scalp infection; nail disease increases with age

rows.label: Clues
items: Pruritus and peripheral scaling; steroid exposure may distort borders and suppress inflammation
★ **Boggy tender scalp plaque** → kerion; inflammatory disease risks permanent scarring alopecia
Interdigital maceration/fissures can become bacterial entry sites

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton digest keratin in stratum corneum, hair, and nails
**T rubrum** most common on skin/nails; capitis → **T tonsurans** (endothrix)
Follicular/deep involvement prevents topical agents from reaching the infected reservoir

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **KOH preparation of active edge** → branching septate hyphae; obtain before systemic treatment when uncertain
Scalp: hair/plucked scale microscopy and culture; nail: clipping KOH, PAS, or fungal culture
Wood lamp detects only selected organisms; negative fluorescence does not exclude tinea
Refractory/widespread infection → reassess diagnosis, adherence, resistance; fungal culture can guide further care

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Limited skin disease → **topical terbinafine** or clotrimazole; continue beyond clinical clearing
★ Hair infection → **oral griseofulvin or terbinafine**; adjunct selenium sulfide/ketoconazole shampoo reduces spread
Nail infection → confirm fungus, then oral terbinafine; baseline liver assessment; counsel slow regrowth
Avoid topical corticosteroid monotherapy or steroid-antifungal combinations; extensive disease may require oral antifungal

rows.label: Complications
items: Secondary cellulitis, persistent nail dystrophy, recurrent infection from untreated reservoirs
Oral antifungals: hepatotoxicity, drug interactions; griseofulvin contraindicated during pregnancy

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Keep feet dry**, change socks, avoid shared towels/combs, disinfect sports gear
Treat symptomatic contacts/pets and coexisting tinea pedis (autoinfects groin → recurrence); avoid barefoot communal-shower exposure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Candida intertrigo: satellite pustules, scrotal involvement
Psoriasis: sharply demarcated plaques, nail pitting; alopecia areata: smooth nonscaly patches

table.title: Site clues
rows: Broken hairs, black dots, patchy alopecia, occipital nodes
Annular plaque, advancing border, central clearing
Thick yellow brittle nail, subungual debris

dermatophyte-infections.evidence: Not checked online; established dermatophyte diagnosis and site-based treatment.

endemic-mycoses.name: Endemic mycoses
endemic-mycoses.scope: Histoplasmosis, blastomycosis, coccidioidomycosis, geographic distribution, itraconazole, amphotericin B
endemic-mycoses.core: Inhaled dimorphic fungi cause pneumonia after geographic exposure; immunosuppression increases dissemination, while morphology distinguishes organisms.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Soil disruption, construction, outdoor work; Histoplasma exposure to bird/bat-enriched soil
HIV, TNF inhibitors, transplant; pregnancy particularly increases severe coccidioidomycosis risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Subacute fever, cough, fatigue, weight loss; nodules or adenopathy may resemble TB/malignancy
Histoplasma dissemination → hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, mucosal lesions or adrenal involvement
Blastomyces → verrucous/ulcerative skin lesions, bone disease
Coccidioides → erythema nodosum/arthralgia; dissemination to skin, bone or meninges

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inhaled environmental spores convert to tissue forms; cellular immunity restricts extrapulmonary spread

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Exposure geography + chest imaging** → organism-directed testing
Histoplasma urine/serum antigen particularly useful in disseminated disease; tissue shows intracellular small yeasts
Coccidioides serology with confirmatory testing; tissue spherules contain endospores
Blastomyces broad-based budding yeast on tissue; culture confirms; antigen cross-reacts with Histoplasma

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Mild self-limited pulmonary histoplasmosis → **observation** in immunocompetent patients
Persistent/worsening histoplasmosis or nonsevere blastomycosis → itraconazole
★ Severe/disseminated histoplasmosis or blastomycosis → **liposomal amphotericin B**, then itraconazole
Uncomplicated cocci often observation; prolonged/severe illness or high-risk host → fluconazole
★ Coccidioidal meningitis → **lifelong fluconazole**; severe nonmeningeal disease → amphotericin induction

rows.label: Complications
items: Histoplasma → fibrosing mediastinitis; disseminated disease → organ failure
Amphotericin → nephrotoxicity, low K/Mg; azoles → liver injury and drug interactions

rows.label: Prevention
items: Dust exposure reduction/respiratory protection; selected profoundly immunosuppressed patients → antifungal prophylaxis

rows.label: Mimics
items: TB: acid-fast testing and mycobacterial culture
Sarcoidosis: noninfectious granulomas; exclude fungi before immunosuppression
Sporotrichosis: thorn/soil inoculation in gardeners → hand papule, **ascending lymphocutaneous nodules**; not inhaled

endemic-mycoses.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [IDSA histoplasmosis 2025](https://www.idsociety.org/practice-guideline/histoplasmosis-2025/); other mycoses: established teaching.

genitourinary-trauma.name: Genitourinary trauma
genitourinary-trauma.scope: Posterior urethral injury, anterior urethral injury, bladder rupture, retrograde urethrography, renal trauma, testicular trauma
genitourinary-trauma.core: Hematuria or inability to void after trauma requires localization of urinary injury before instrumentation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pelvic fracture → posterior urethra/bladder; straddle injury → anterior bulbar urethra
Deceleration, flank impact or penetrating wounds → renal/collecting-system injury
Blunt scrotal trauma → testicular rupture; empty bladder better protected than distended bladder
Hysterectomy/pelvic surgery → ureteral ligation: flank pain, fever, unilateral hydroureteronephrosis; not pyelonephritis

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Blood at urethral meatus**, retention, perineal/scrotal hematoma or high-riding prostate → urethral injury
Gross hematuria with pelvic fracture → suspect bladder rupture
Flank ecchymosis, tenderness or lower rib fractures suggest renal injury
Scrotal swelling, bruising and loss of normal contour suggest testicular rupture

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Pelvic shearing disrupts membranous urethra; direct compression splits the bulbar segment
Intraperitoneal urine leakage irritates peritoneum; blood loss can cause shock despite modest hematuria

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected urethral injury → **retrograde urethrogram before Foley**; no blind repeated attempts
★ Stable gross hematuria + pelvic fracture → **retrograde CT/plain cystography**
Blunt flank trauma → **urinalysis**; stable, no hematuria → **no further testing** unless high-energy deceleration
Stable gross hematuria, or microscopic + hypotension → contrast CT abdomen/pelvis with delayed images, not laparotomy
Testicular injury → Doppler ultrasound; absent flow or high clinical suspicion → immediate exploration

rows.label: Tx
items: Hemodynamic instability → trauma resuscitation and urgent operative/angiographic hemorrhage control
Urethral disruption → urology, suprapubic drainage or selected endoscopic realignment
★ **Intraperitoneal bladder rupture → surgical repair**; uncomplicated extraperitoneal rupture → catheter drainage
Stable renal injuries → observation; ongoing arterial bleeding → selective embolization
Testicular rupture → urgent exploration, repair and removal of nonviable tissue

rows.label: Complications
items: Urethral stricture, erectile dysfunction, incontinence; urinary extravasation → infection or urinoma
Delayed renal bleeding, hypertension or kidney loss; testicular atrophy and infertility

rows.label: Prevention
items: Protective equipment; safe catheter technique; follow-up for stricture after urethral injury

rows.label: Mimics
items: Testicular torsion: absent flow with spermatic-cord twist; also surgical emergency
Nontraumatic stone: colicky flank pain without injury mechanism

hiv-infection.name: HIV infection
hiv-infection.scope: Acute HIV, testing, ART start, opportunistic infection prophylaxis, PrEP/PEP, opportunistic infections (CMV retinitis, toxoplasmosis, PJP)
hiv-infection.core: HIV progressively depletes CD4 cells; early diagnosis and suppressive ART prevent immune failure and sexual transmission.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sexual exposure, shared injection equipment, perinatal transmission; other STIs increase acquisition risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Acute infection 2–4 weeks post-exposure: fever, rash, sore throat, **mucosal ulcers**, diarrhea, generalized lymphadenopathy
Weight loss, thrush, recurrent candida/herpes, **extensive adult molluscum** → test HIV; dysphagia → candidal esophagitis
Child/teen: chronic fever/diarrhea, poor growth, generalized nodes, splenomegaly, **polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Retroviral integration creates lifelong reservoirs; ongoing replication drives immune depletion and inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Fourth-generation Ag/Ab → HIV-1/2 differentiation assay**; discordance → HIV RNA
★ Recent exposure/acute syndrome despite negative screen → **HIV RNA**, before antibodies appear
Baseline viral load, CD4, genotype, renal/liver function, HBV/HCV/TB, pregnancy testing, **cervical cytology**
AIDS: CD4 <200 or AIDS-defining illness regardless of count
Prenatal: opt-out screening; refusal → counsel, re-offer later; never test without consent

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Start **integrase-based ART promptly**, usually bictegravir/TAF/emtricitabine; assess HBV coinfection and interactions
Do not delay routine ART for genotype; cryptococcal/TB meningitis require disease-specific deferred timing
PJP: TMP-SMX; add glucocorticoid if PaO₂ <70 or A–a gradient ≥35
Toxoplasmosis: **pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine/leucovorin**, else TMP-SMX; CMV retinitis: valganciclovir, ophthalmology
Untreated/viremic mother's newborn → **triple ART** ASAP, ideally within 6 h, ≤6 weeks; suppressed mother → zidovudine alone

rows.label: Complications
items: Opportunistic infections, malignancies, wasting, neurocognitive disease, kidney disease
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome after ART; drug toxicity/interactions

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ PJP prophylaxis: **TMP-SMX** with CD4 <200 before/starting ART; on ART, <100 or 100–200 with viremia
Toxoplasma IgG positive + CD4 <100 → prophylaxis; MAC <50 only without immediate effective ART
★ Exposure ≤72 hours → **28-day PEP: dolutegravir + TDF/emtricitabine**; do not delay for laboratory results
PrEP: TDF/emtricitabine, cabotegravir, or lenacapavir; exclude HIV first, continue serial testing

rows.label: Mimics
items: EBV mononucleosis: atypical lymphocytes, heterophile positivity; acute HIV can be heterophile-negative
Primary CNS lymphoma: often solitary lesion; biopsy after failed empiric anti-Toxoplasma treatment, earlier if serology/imaging/CSF PCR disagree
SCID/CVID: low immunoglobulins; SCID lymphopenia, no nodes; perinatal HIV: PJP, thrush, nodes, normal lymphocytes

table.title: Advanced-disease syndromes
rows: Dry cough, hypoxemia, ground-glass; sputum/BAL silver stain
Ring-enhancing mass lesions, edema/mass effect; positive IgG
Cognitive decline; non-enhancing subcortical demyelination, no mass effect

hyperthyroidism.name: Hyperthyroidism and thyrotoxicosis
hyperthyroidism.scope: Graves disease, toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma, subacute thyroiditis, thyroid storm, beta-blockers, thionamides, radioactive iodine
hyperthyroidism.core: Excess circulating thyroid hormone → heat intolerance, weight loss despite appetite, tremor, and tachycardia; hormone overproduction differs from destructive release.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune history, female sex; older age favors autonomous nodules
Iodine load, amiodarone, exogenous thyroid hormone; infection/surgery can precipitate storm

rows.label: Clues
items: Hyperreflexia, lid lag, onycholysis, frequent stools, proximal weakness, widened pulse pressure; older adults: apathetic
★ **Thyroid storm**: fever, delirium, severe tachyarrhythmia, vomiting, heart failure; clinical diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Increased tissue metabolic activity and beta-adrenergic sensitivity explain systemic manifestations
Thionamides block thyroid peroxidase; PTU also reduces peripheral T4 → T3 conversion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TSH first → free T4**, total T3 if T4 normal; suppressed TSH with elevated hormones
TRAb establishes Graves; uncertain cause → **Doppler ultrasound** or radioiodine uptake (not if pregnant/lactating)
Low uptake: thyroiditis/exogenous hormone; low thyroglobulin supports exogenous ingestion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptom control: **propranolol**; caution in asthma or decompensated HF
★ Storm → ICU, cooling/fluids, beta-blockade if tolerated, **PTU → iodine ≥1 hour later**, hydrocortisone
Radioiodine contraindicated during pregnancy/lactation; significant active orbitopathy favors another definitive treatment
Compression/suspicious nodule → thyroidectomy after control; pregnancy: first-trimester PTU, later methimazole

rows.label: Complications
items: AF, embolism, osteoporosis, mild hypercalcemia, cardiomyopathy; radioiodine often → hypothyroidism
★ Thionamides: **fever/sore throat → stop drug, urgent CBC**; PTU → severe hepatotoxicity
Pregnancy: thionamides/TRAb cross placenta → **fetal goiter**, impaired swallowing, polyhydramnios

rows.label: Prevention
items: Monitor free T4 early during treatment; TSH recovery lags
Smoking cessation for orbitopathy; definitive treatment before planned pregnancy when feasible

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic disorder: episodic symptoms without thyroid biochemical abnormalities
Pheochromocytoma: paroxysmal headache, sweating, severe hypertension
Menopause: hot flashes with menstrual transition, normal thyroid testing
Orbital pseudotumor: involves muscle bellies and tendons; Graves spares tendons

table.title: Etiology determines treatment
rows: Diffuse uptake; bruit, orbitopathy, pretibial myxedema, acropachy (clubbing)
One hot nodule, suppressed surrounding tissue
NSAID; prednisone if severe; no thionamides

hyponatremia.name: Hyponatremia
hyponatremia.scope: Hypovolemic, euvolemic (SIADH, primary polydipsia), hypervolemic, acute vs chronic, hypertonic saline indications
hyponatremia.core: Low serum sodium reflects excess water relative to sodium; symptoms and duration determine urgency before the cause determines maintenance treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Thiazides, SSRIs, carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine, oxytocin; **hypotonic IV D5W**, postoperative state, exercise + excess water
Pulmonary/CNS disease; **small cell lung cancer** (ectopic ADH); heart failure, cirrhosis, renal failure

rows.label: Clues
items: Nausea, headache, gait instability; seizures, coma or marked confusion indicate severe cerebral edema
Orthostasis/dry mucosa suggest depletion; edema/ascites suggest excess extracellular fluid
SIADH: clinically euvolemic with inappropriately concentrated urine despite hypo-osmolality
Massive water intake, often psychiatric illness; urine osmolality below serum still favors polydipsia, even if >100

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Hypotonic extracellular fluid drives water into brain; chronic adaptation makes rapid correction dangerous
ADH-mediated water retention or intake exceeding renal dilution capacity lowers sodium concentration
Low effective volume (heart failure, cirrhosis, diarrhea) → baroreceptor ADH release; total-body sodium high in edema

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Serum osmolality first: **<275 mOsm/kg** confirms hypotonicity; assess glucose and volume status
Hyperglycemia → translocational hyponatremia; severe hyperlipidemia/proteinemia → pseudohyponatremia
★ Urine osmolality **<100** → polydipsia/low solute; ≥100 → persistent ADH activity
Urine Na <20–30 suggests low effective arterial volume; >30 suggests renal loss or SIADH
Exclude adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism and renal failure before diagnosing SIADH; diuretics confound urine Na

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe neurologic symptoms → **3% saline bolus**, repeated for initial Na rise 4–6 mEq/L
Hypovolemia → isotonic saline; SIADH → fluid restriction, increased solute, remove trigger
Edematous states → fluid/sodium restriction and loop diuretic; treat heart/liver/kidney disorder
★ Chronic/unknown duration: generally limit rise to **≤8 mEq/L per 24 h**; monitor frequently
Overcorrection → desmopressin plus D5W; avoid routine vaptans in acute symptomatic cases

rows.label: Complications
items: Acute severe hyponatremia → herniation, respiratory arrest
Osmotic demyelination after rapid correction; greatest risk with alcoholism, malnutrition, hypokalemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid hypotonic maintenance fluids during high ADH states; review causative drugs
Monitor for brisk aquaresis after restoring volume or stopping thiazides

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cerebral salt wasting: neurosurgical patient, hypovolemic, high urine Na; SIADH euvolemic
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemia: measured osmolality elevated
Primary psychiatric disease: neurologic change without sodium abnormality

hyponatremia.evidence: Not checked online; established hyponatremia consensus principles.

infant-nutrition.name: Infant nutrition
infant-nutrition.scope: Exclusive breastfeeding recommendations, vitamin D supplementation, introduction of solid foods, cow milk protein allergy (hydrolyzed formula), formula types
infant-nutrition.core: Breast milk or iron-fortified infant formula anchors first-year nutrition; add supplements and complementary foods according to developmental readiness.

rows.label: Who
items: All infants; assess growth, feeding effectiveness, urine output, and family feeding preferences

rows.label: Schedule
items: ★ **Exclusive breastfeeding about 6 months**; continue with complementary foods through 2 years or longer
★ Solids around **6 months**, never before 4; head control, sitting, diminished extrusion reflex
Begin iron-rich meat or fortified cereal; advance textures; introduce allergens without unnecessary delay

rows.label: Special groups
items: ★ Breastfed/partially breastfed → **vitamin D 400 IU/day** from shortly after birth
Formula-only: vitamin D supplement until intake ≥32 oz/day
Exclusively breastfed term infants: **iron 1 mg/kg/day from 4 months** until adequate dietary iron

rows.label: Choice
items: Blood-streaked stool, eczema, emesis → milk-protein allergy; confirm elimination/rechallenge
Breastfed proctocolitis → maternal dairy elimination, dietitian; persistent symptoms → eliminate soy
Proctocolitis: non-IgE, usually outgrown by age 1–3; lactose intolerance: no bloody stool

rows.label: Contraindications
items: No **honey before 12 months**; avoid choking hazards and unpasteurized foods
No cow milk as primary drink before 12 months; no homemade/diluted formula
Classic galactosemia → avoid breast milk and lactose-containing formula

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **Lactose-free ≠ hypoallergenic**; avoid partial hydrolysates/goat milk for milk-protein allergy
Severe eczema/egg allergy → peanut evaluation and introduction at 4–6 months
No cereal in bottles; responsive feeding, no forced finishing

informed-consent-and-capacity.name: Informed consent and capacity
informed-consent-and-capacity.scope: Decision-making capacity, informed consent, emergency exception (implied consent), refusal of treatment, AMA discharge
informed-consent-and-capacity.core: A capable adult may accept or refuse treatment after understanding its benefits, material risks, alternatives, and consequences of refusal.

rows.label: Principle
items: ★ Capacity: **understand, appreciate (own case), reason, communicate**; decision-specific, fluctuating
Competence: legal; diagnosis, age, alcohol use, incarceration, disagreement alone ≠ incapacity

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Explain benefits, material risks, alternatives/no treatment; **qualified interpreter and teach-back**
Correct delirium, intoxication, pain, communication barriers; reassess capacity
AMA request: assess capacity, explore barriers, offer safer plan, document discussion and follow-up

rows.label: Don't
items: Capable refusal → respect choice, even if life-saving or pregnant; avoid coercion, abandonment
No valid consent → possible **battery**; signed form alone insufficient
Refusing one therapy (blood) ≠ refusing all; provide other indicated care, including surgery

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ Emergency + incapacity + no surrogate/directive/verified refusal → implied consent to treat
★ Parents refuse minor's life-saving transfusion → **treat emergency**; seek court authority if feasible
Incapacity without emergency → authorized surrogate; involve patient to remaining ability

rows.label: Traps
items: Psychiatric illness does not automatically remove capacity; assess the specific decision
Suicide danger may justify protective detention despite expressed desire to leave
New material procedure or changed risk → renewed consent; consent revocable anytime before procedure

table.title: Who decides
rows: Ask whom to involve; facilitate promptly; no override
Minor decides; no parental consent (state law varies)
Parents seek unproven remedy for child
Continue proven therapy; investigate remedy; CPS not first
Close; discuss after waking; no next-of-kin consent
Autonomy ≠ entitlement; physician refuses, explains, offers alternatives

informed-consent-and-capacity.evidence: Not checked online; established consent/capacity ethics; emergency and minor-consent law varies by jurisdiction.

knee-injuries.name: Knee injuries
knee-injuries.scope: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tear, posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) tear, collateral ligaments, meniscal tears, knee dislocation, popliteal artery injury, Ottawa knee rules
knee-injuries.core: Knee trauma assessment starts with neurovascular safety and fracture risk, then uses mechanism, effusion timing, and targeted ligament or meniscal tests.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Pivoting/cutting sports, contact trauma, dashboard impact, hyperextension
Older age, osteoporosis, and inability to bear weight increase fracture probability

rows.label: Clues
items: Immediate large effusion suggests hemarthrosis; delayed swelling and catching suggest meniscal injury
★ **Gross deformity or spontaneously reduced dislocation** → popliteal artery injury risk
Cool foot, weak pulses, paresthesia, escalating pain → vascular compromise or compartment syndrome

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ligament disruption → instability; displaced meniscal fragment → mechanical locking
Knee dislocation may stretch/tear popliteal artery despite restored alignment and initially palpable pulses

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Neurovascular examination before and after reduction**; ABI assesses arterial injury
★ ABI **<0.9, abnormal pulses, or pre-reduction deficit → CT angiography**; hard ischemic signs → vascular intervention
Normal ABI/pulses, no prior deficit → serial vascular checks, not immediate discharge
Ottawa: age ≥55, isolated patellar/fibular-head tenderness, flexion <90°, or inability four-step weight-bearing → radiographs
MRI for soft-tissue injury after fracture evaluation; locked knee → prompt orthopedic assessment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Dislocation → **urgent reduction before angiography**, immobilization, orthopedic/vascular consultation
Initial sprain → ice/compression, analgesia, protected weight bearing then early rehabilitation
Isolated collateral sprain → hinged brace + rehabilitation; many PCL injuries managed nonoperatively
ACL rupture with athletic demands/persistent instability or combined injury → reconstruction discussion
Displaced locked meniscal tear → arthroscopy; degenerative tears without locking usually exercise-based rehabilitation

rows.label: Complications
items: Missed arterial injury → limb loss; peroneal nerve injury → foot drop
Chronic instability, recurrent meniscal injury, posttraumatic osteoarthritis, stiffness

rows.label: Prevention
items: Neuromuscular landing/pivot training, strength and balance rehabilitation before sport return

rows.label: Mimics
items: Patellar dislocation: lateral patellar displacement, often spontaneous reduction
Septic arthritis: atraumatic hot effusion, fever; urgent aspiration
Patellofemoral pain/instability: running, stairs, sitting → anterior pain; crepitus, genu valgum, lax patella; no effusion unless acute dislocation
Osgood-Schlatter: growth-spurt athlete, chronic tibial tubercle pain; traction apophysitis, tendon-insertion microfractures

table.title: Mechanism and examination
rows: Joint-line tenderness; McMurray: click on rotation/extension; Thessaly

knee-injuries.evidence: Not checked online; established orthopedic trauma and Ottawa knee principles.

meckel-diverticulum.name: Meckel diverticulum
meckel-diverticulum.scope: Persistent vitelline duct, ectopic gastric mucosa, painless lower GI bleeding, technetium-99m pertechnetate scan, intussusception, surgical resection
meckel-diverticulum.core: A congenital ileal remnant can present with childhood intestinal bleeding, obstruction, or appendicitis-like inflammation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Persistent **vitelline/omphalomesenteric duct**; congenital lesion, symptomatic disease more common in boys
Ectopic gastric tissue increases bleeding; complications often arise in childhood, but possible at any age

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Painless maroon or bright-red rectal bleeding** in an otherwise well child
Colicky pain, vomiting or obstruction when serving as an intussusception lead point
Diverticulitis → fever, RLQ pain and tenderness; perforation produces peritoneal signs
Large-volume blood loss → pallor, tachycardia or shock; benign abdominal examination does not ensure mild disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: True diverticulum contains all bowel-wall layers, usually antimesenteric distal ileum
Acid secretion from heterotopic gastric mucosa ulcerates adjacent ileal lining

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspected bleeding Meckel → **technetium-99m pertechnetate scan**, detects gastric mucosa
Negative scan does not exclude lesion without sufficient ectopic tissue; pediatric sensitivity exceeds adult sensitivity
Ultrasound if intussusception suspected; CT for inflammatory/obstructive presentations or alternative diagnoses
CBC, type/crossmatch for substantial bleeding; endoscopic studies may be unrevealing because lesion lies beyond routine reach

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Brisk bleeding/shock → **IV access, crystalloid/blood**, urgent pediatric/surgical consultation
★ Symptomatic lesion → **diverticulectomy or segmental ileal resection**, including adjacent ulcerated bowel
Perforation/peritonitis → broad-spectrum antibiotics and urgent operation; obstruction → NPO and decompression
Incidentally found asymptomatic lesion → individualized surgical decision based on risk and operative context

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent hemorrhage and anemia, intussusception, volvulus around fibrous band, bowel ischemia
Diverticulitis or perforation; postoperative adhesions can cause later small-bowel obstruction

rows.label: Mimics
items: Juvenile polyp: painless bleeding but intraluminal colonic lesion on colonoscopy
Anal fissure: painful stooling with surface streaks; peptic bleeding: upper-GI source

meckel-diverticulum.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

microcytic-anemia.name: Microcytic anemia
microcytic-anemia.scope: Iron deficiency, anemia of chronic disease, thalassemia, sideroblastic anemia
microcytic-anemia.core: Low hemoglobin with MCV <80 fL: distinguish depleted iron, inflammatory iron sequestration, globin underproduction, and defective heme synthesis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Menstrual/GI blood loss, pregnancy, low intake, malabsorption → iron depletion
Chronic infection, autoimmune disease, malignancy → inflammatory anemia
Inherited hemoglobin disorders; alcohol, lead, isoniazid, myelodysplasia → disordered heme production
Preterm birth → low stores, screen toddlers; infant microcytosis → **dietary history** for excess cow's milk

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, pallor, exertional dyspnea; severe anemia → tachycardia, angina, syncope
Pica, koilonychia, restless legs suggest iron deficiency
Markedly low MCV, preserved hemoglobin, high RBC count, **normal RDW** (Mentzer <13) suggest thalassemia trait

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inflammation → ↑hepcidin → ferroportin suppression, impaired absorption and iron release; cytokines blunt **erythropoietin**
Sideroblasts: mitochondrial iron accumulation in erythroblasts from impaired protoporphyrin synthesis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CBC/smear → ferritin**, iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation; ferritin rises with inflammation
★ Ferritin **<45 ng/mL in anemia** supports iron deficiency; normal result cannot exclude during inflammation
★ Adult men/postmenopausal women with iron deficiency → **EGD + colonoscopy**; consider celiac testing
Hemoglobin electrophoresis for suspected beta-thalassemia; alpha trait may require genetic testing; exposure → blood lead
Microcytosis + afebrile pain crisis, at-risk ancestry → **smear** for sickled cells (sickle–β-thalassemia)

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Iron deficiency → **oral ferrous sulfate**; intolerance/malabsorption or rapid replacement need → IV iron
Treat bleeding source; continue iron about 3 months beyond hemoglobin normalization; reassess nonresponse
Inflammatory anemia → treat underlying disease; selected CKD → iron ± erythropoietin
Sideroblastic: remove trigger, pyridoxine if isoniazid-related; severe thalassemia → transfusion/chelation

rows.label: Complications
items: Iron deficiency: developmental effects in children, adverse pregnancy outcomes
Repeated transfusion → iron overload, cardiac/hepatic injury; oral iron → constipation, dark stool
Four-gene α-deletion → **Hb Barts** (γ4) → severe fetal anemia, hydrops fetalis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Adequate dietary iron, pregnancy supplementation, lead-exposure reduction
★ **No empiric long-term iron for thalassemia trait** without documented deficiency

rows.label: Mimics
items: Acute blood loss: initially normocytic; hemoglobin may lag volume loss
Hemolysis: reticulocytosis, ↑LDH/indirect bilirubin, ↓haptoglobin

microcytic-anemia.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [AGA iron deficiency evaluation 2020](https://gastro.org/clinical-guidance/gastrointestinal-evaluation-of-iron-deficiency-anemia/); remaining hematology established teaching.

neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.name: Neonatal intestinal obstruction
neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.scope: Malrotation with midgut volvulus, duodenal atresia, jejunoileal atresia, meconium ileus, Hirschsprung disease, bilious vomiting, upper GI contrast series, Ladd procedure
neonatal-intestinal-obstruction.core: Bilious vomiting in a neonate is intestinal obstruction until proved otherwise; volvulus must be excluded before bowel ischemia develops.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Polyhydramnios → prenatal proximal obstruction; Down syndrome → duodenal atresia
CF → meconium ileus; trisomy 21 → Hirschsprung disease
Prematurity increases alternative risk of necrotizing enterocolitis

rows.label: Clues
items: Proximal obstruction → early vomiting with little distention; distal obstruction → marked distention
No meconium by **48 hours**, explosive stool after rectal exam → distal aganglionosis
★ Bloody stool, tenderness, shock or metabolic acidosis → ischemic bowel; urgent surgery
Volvulus: sudden bilious emesis after normal feeding and meconium; atresia: vomiting from first feeds

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Malrotation leaves narrow mesenteric base → twisting of bowel and mesenteric blood supply
Duodenal atresia: failed recanalization; jejunoileal atresia: fetal vascular injury
Hirschsprung: absent enteric ganglia → failure of distal relaxation and proximal dilation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Abdominal radiograph** first; double bubble without distal gas supports duodenal atresia
★ Suspected malrotation, stable → **upper GI contrast series**; corkscrew/abnormal DJ junction; enema: misplaced cecum
Distal obstruction → contrast enema to characterize microcolon, meconium or transition zone
Hirschsprung confirmation → **rectal suction biopsy**, absent ganglion cells
Peritonitis or unstable suspected volvulus → exploration without delaying for contrast

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ All suspected obstruction → **NPO, orogastric decompression, IV fluids**, pediatric surgery
Volvulus → emergency Ladd procedure, detorsion and viability assessment; broad antibiotics if ischemic
Atresias → operative repair after stabilization; duodenal repair commonly duodenoduodenostomy
Uncomplicated meconium ileus → water-soluble contrast enema with hydration; complicated cases → surgery
Hirschsprung → irrigations then pull-through; enterocolitis → fluids, decompression, IV broad antibiotics

rows.label: Complications
items: Bowel necrosis, perforation, sepsis, short-bowel syndrome; Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis can be fatal
Delayed diagnosis causes aspiration, electrolyte depletion and growth failure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pyloric stenosis: nonbilious projectile emesis at several weeks
NEC: ill preterm infant, pneumatosis intestinalis
Physiologic reflux: thriving infant without bile or distention

table.title: Distal obstruction clues
rows: Narrow distal segment, proximal transition zone

neonatal-resuscitation.name: Neonatal resuscitation
neonatal-resuscitation.scope: NRP algorithm, initial steps (warm, dry, stimulate), PPV indications (apnea, HR < 100), chest compressions (HR < 60), epinephrine, target SpO2
neonatal-resuscitation.core: At birth, effective ventilation drives heart-rate recovery; escalate support according to the response after each timed intervention.

rows.label: Definition
items: Apgar: appearance, pulse, grimace, activity, respiration, each scored 0–2 at 1 and 5 min
Score 1: acrocyanosis, pulse <100, grimace, some flexion, irregular breathing

rows.label: Interpret
items: ★ **Right-hand preductal pulse oximetry**; targets: 2 min 65–70%, 5 min 80–85%, 10 min 85–95%
Auscultate HR initially; ECG improves continuous measurement during advanced support
Oxygen start: ≥35 wk **21%**; 32–34 wk 21–30%; <32 wk 30–100%, titrated

rows.label: Use when
items: Vigorous term newborn → skin-to-skin, routine care; defer cord clamping ≥60 seconds
★ Poor tone/breathing → **warm, dry, position airway, stimulate**; initial assessment within first minute
Spontaneous breathing plus distress/cyanosis → oxygen titration; consider CPAP

rows.label: Compare
items: ★ Poor PPV → **reposition, reseal, open mouth, suction obstruction, raise pressure, alternate airway**
Compressions: two-thumb encircling technique, depth one-third chest; 90 compressions + 30 breaths/min
Epinephrine: **0.01–0.03 mg/kg IV/IO**; repeat every 3–5 min; umbilical venous access preferred

rows.label: Traps
items: No routine suction, including meconium; suction only suspected airway obstruction
★ **2025 PPV rate 30–60/min**; older teaching 40–60/min
Persistent bradycardia → check pneumothorax/hypovolemia; blood loss → saline or uncrossmatched blood

table.title: Timed escalation
rows: Stop compressions; continue ventilation if needed

neonatal-sepsis.name: Neonatal sepsis
neonatal-sepsis.scope: Early-onset neonatal sepsis, late-onset neonatal sepsis, Group B Streptococcus, Listeria, ampicillin and gentamicin
neonatal-sepsis.core: A newborn with temperature instability, feeding difficulty, apnea, or unexplained deterioration may have invasive infection despite subtle examination findings.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Prematurity, maternal GBS, membrane rupture ≥18 hours**, intra-amniotic infection
Late disease: central lines, ventilation, prolonged hospitalization, disrupted skin/GI barriers

rows.label: Clues
items: Hypothermia or fever, lethargy, irritability, poor suck, jaundice, vomiting or glucose instability
Respiratory distress, desaturation, mottling, delayed capillary refill; hypotension is a late sign
Bulging fontanelle or seizures suggest meningitis; vesicles, hepatitis or maternal HSV suggest herpes

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immature innate/adaptive immunity permits rapid hematogenous spread
Maternal genital organisms seed early disease; later acquisition includes community and healthcare organisms

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Ill neonate → **blood culture before antibiotics**, CBC and inflammatory markers as adjuncts
LP when safe for suspected meningitis, positive blood culture, critical illness or poor response
Urine culture useful in late-onset evaluation; not routinely needed for immediate early-onset disease
Never delay antibiotics for LP in instability; normal WBC/CRP does not exclude infection

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Early-onset empiric treatment → **ampicillin + gentamicin** after cultures
Suspected meningitis → ampicillin plus cefotaxime where available, tailored to local resistance and cultures
NICU late-onset disease → antistaphylococcal plus gram-negative coverage; vancomycin when MRSA/line resistance risk
★ HSV concern → **IV acyclovir** plus HSV testing; avoid ceftriaxone in neonates
Respiratory/perfusion support; if cultures negative and infant well, stop empiric antibiotics at 36–48 hours

rows.label: Complications
items: Septic shock, DIC, meningitis, hearing loss, neurodevelopmental injury or death
Gentamicin → renal/ototoxicity; unnecessary antibiotics alter microbiome and increase resistant infection risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Maternal **GBS screening and intrapartum penicillin** for positive/eligible high-risk mothers
Hand/line hygiene; well exposed infants ≥35 weeks → serial exams or sepsis-risk calculator strategy

rows.label: Mimics
items: RDS/TTN: delivery-related respiratory pattern without systemic infection evidence
Hypoglycemia or duct-dependent cardiac disease: metabolic/cardiac testing identifies cause

table.title: Common organisms
rows: GBS (most common), E coli; less often Listeria
Coagulase-negative staphylococci, S aureus, gram-negatives, Candida
GBS, E coli, other enteric bacteria

nephrotic-syndrome.name: Nephrotic syndrome
nephrotic-syndrome.scope: Minimal change, FSGS, membranous, diabetic nephropathy; thrombosis and hyperlipidemia
nephrotic-syndrome.core: Heavy proteinuria with hypoalbuminemia and edema indicates nephrotic syndrome; assess the cause and complications before choosing immunosuppression.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Diabetes, obesity, HIV, hepatitis B/C, autoimmune disease, malignancy and selected medications
Children favor minimal change; obesity, HIV, heroin or reduced nephron mass can cause secondary FSGS

rows.label: Clues
items: Periorbital/dependent edema, foamy urine, weight gain; severe cases → anasarca or effusions
Hyperlipidemia, lipiduria, oval fat bodies/fatty casts; urine sediment often otherwise bland
★ Sudden flank pain, hematuria or falling filtration → **renal vein thrombosis**
Low effective volume may coexist with overload; edema gone + orthostasis/oliguria on diuretic → **overdiuresis**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Podocyte barrier damage leaks albumin; sodium retention and low oncotic pressure promote edema
Urinary loss of anticoagulants and immunoglobulins increases thrombosis and infection risk

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Adult protein **>3.5 g/day** or equivalent spot protein/creatinine ratio; serum albumin and lipid profile
Urinalysis/microscopy, renal function, HbA1c; targeted HIV, HBV/HCV, ANA/complement and monoclonal-protein studies
★ Most unexplained adult cases → **kidney biopsy**; classic childhood minimal change often treated empirically
Anti-PLA2R supports primary membranous disease; assess secondary causes and age-based cancer screening
Diabetes with retinopathy, gradually rising albuminuria → likely diabetic nephropathy; atypical features → consider biopsy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Salt restriction, **loop diuretic**, ACE inhibitor/ARB for proteinuria; monitor perfusion and K
Eligible CKD → SGLT2 inhibitor; treat diabetes/infection or remove causative drug
Minimal change/primary FSGS → glucocorticoids; secondary FSGS → cause-directed/supportive treatment, not routine steroids
Membranous disease → risk-stratified observation versus rituximab or other immunosuppression
★ Confirmed thrombosis → anticoagulate; preventive anticoagulation individualized by albumin, pathology and bleeding risk

rows.label: Complications
items: DVT/PE, renal vein thrombosis, cellulitis/peritonitis, AKI, accelerated atherosclerosis
Progressive glomerular scarring can lead to kidney failure

rows.label: Prevention
items: Vaccinate, control BP/glycemia, avoid NSAIDs; monitor treatment toxicity and recurrent proteinuria

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nephritic syndrome: dysmorphic RBCs/casts, hypertension, inflammatory sediment
Cirrhosis: low albumin without nephrotic protein loss

table.title: Classic pathology
rows: Diffuse foot-process effacement; normal light microscopy

nephrotic-syndrome.evidence: Not checked online; established nephrology teaching and risk-based treatment principles.

newborn-screening.name: Newborn screening
newborn-screening.scope: Congenital hypothyroidism (macroglossia, umbilical hernia, levothyroxine), phenylketonuria, galactosemia, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, hemoglobinopathies, cystic fibrosis, pulse oximetry, hearing screen
newborn-screening.core: Screen apparently healthy newborns for treatable metabolic, endocrine, genetic, cardiac, and hearing disorders before symptoms or irreversible injury.

rows.label: Who
items: All newborns; blood-spot panels vary by state; also screen cardiac oxygenation and hearing

rows.label: Start/stop
items: ★ Heel stick **24–48 hours**; early collection, transfusion, prematurity may require repeats
Pulse oximetry ≥24 hours or before early discharge; hearing by 1 month

rows.label: Test
items: ★ Cardiac pass: **≥95% in both right hand and foot**, difference ≤3 percentage points
<90% anywhere → immediate failure; otherwise **one repeat** in 1 hour (older algorithms: two)
Hearing: otoacoustic emissions or auditory brainstem response; NICU → brainstem-based screen

rows.label: IF positive
items: ★ Critical result → confirm promptly without delaying lifesaving treatment
Failed cardiac screen → evaluate hypoxemia, echocardiography; ductal-dependent lesion → prostaglandin E1
★ Failed hearing → diagnostic audiology by **3 months**, intervention by **6 months**

rows.label: Traps
items: Normal examination does not exclude disease; hypothyroidism later causes macroglossia/umbilical hernia
Ill infant with suspected CAH → treat despite pending screen; no diagnostic reassurance
Hereditary fructose intolerance: symptoms only after fructose/sucrose, so not on breast milk alone

table.title: Urgent positive blood-spot results
rows: Start levothyroxine promptly, ideally by 2 weeks
Classic galactosemia: feeding → vomiting, jaundice, hepatomegaly
Penicillin from infancy, vaccines, hematology follow-up
Specialty care, nutrition, pancreatic enzymes if insufficient

newborn-screening.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [CDC cardiac screening](https://www.cdc.gov/heart-defects/hcp/screening/), [CDC hearing](https://www.cdc.gov/hearing-loss-children/screening/); blood-spot actions established teaching.

normal-pediatric-variants.name: Normal pediatric variants
normal-pediatric-variants.scope: Thymic sail sign on chest radiograph, physiologic genu varum and valgum, tibial torsion, infantile hemangioma
normal-pediatric-variants.core: Age-appropriate anatomy and growth can resemble disease; symmetry, normal function, and expected evolution support reassurance instead of unnecessary intervention.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Normal skeletal alignment changes with development; familial rotational profiles are common
Infantile hemangiomas more frequent with prematurity, low birth weight and female sex

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Symmetric painless findings with normal growth/function** favor physiologic variation
Asymmetry, pain, progression, short stature or abnormal neurologic examination → pathologic evaluation
Hemangiomas appear in first weeks, proliferate rapidly during infancy, then gradually involute
Periocular, airway/beard-distribution, ulcerating or large segmental lesions are high-risk, not simple cosmetic variants

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Growth remodels lower-limb alignment/rotation; normal thymic tissue may silhouette against the lung
Hemangioma is a benign vascular tumor with proliferative and involution phases, distinct from vascular malformation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical symmetric limb variant → **clinical examination**, growth review and rotational profile
Imaging for red flags, atypical age or suspected metabolic bone disease; not routine physiologic bowing
Typical hemangioma → clinical diagnosis; ≥5 cutaneous lesions → hepatic ultrasound
Large segmental facial/lumbosacral lesion → evaluate associated structural anomalies with specialist guidance

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Reassurance and observation** for physiologic alignment, thymic appearance, toddler genital self-touching without abuse signs
Special shoes/braces do not correct internal tibial torsion; persistent severe functional deformity → orthopedics
★ High-risk hemangioma → **early referral, oral propranolol**; selected superficial lesions → topical timolol
Give propranolol with feeds, hold during poor intake/vomiting; monitor bradycardia and hypoglycemia

rows.label: Complications
items: Unnecessary imaging, bracing or surgery; hemangioma → ulceration, amblyopia, airway obstruction or residual skin change
Multiple hepatic hemangiomas → high-output heart failure or consumptive hypothyroidism

rows.label: Mimics
items: Blount disease: progressive asymmetric tibial bowing; rickets: widened wrists, abnormal mineralization
Mediastinal mass: mass effect/distortion rather than soft thymic contour

normal-pediatric-variants.evidence: Hemangioma guidance checked 2026-10-30: [AAP 2019 guideline](https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/143/1/e20183475/37268/Clinical-Practice-Guideline-for-the-Management-of); skeletal variants: established teaching.
